subject: paediatrics
title: Neonatal infections, jaundice and metabolic care

steps.tx: Early onset **sepsis** in a newborn follows infection with group B streptococcus or Escherichia coli, often after prolonged rupture of membranes. The baby may show lethargy, poor feeding and **temperature instability** rather than clear fever. The team takes cultures first and starts **ampicillin with gentamicin**, adding cefotaxime when meningitis is suspected. Antibiotics stop after 36 to 48 hours when cultures stay negative and the baby looks well.
steps.say: A newborn with early infection often looks dull and feeds very poorly. The temperature may swing high or low instead of showing a steady fever. Doctors collect blood cultures before they start the first antibiotic dose. The usual early treatment will cover the common bacteria that infect newborn babies. Treatment stops early when cultures remain negative and the baby recovers well.

steps.tx: Jaundice on the first day, yellow palms and soles, or a rapid rise in bilirubin signals **pathologic jaundice** rather than a normal pattern. Physiologic jaundice appears on day 2 to 4 in a term baby, as the chart in this figure helps to judge. The team checks the **Bhutani** hour based level, blood group mismatch and **glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase** status. Phototherapy treats most babies, while exchange transfusion and immunoglobulin serve severe isoimmune disease.
steps.say: The chart will plot bilirubin against the age of the baby in hours. A level that rises too fast or appears on the first day needs urgent attention. Yellow colour on the palms and soles can also warn the doctor about severe disease. Light therapy breaks down bilirubin through the skin of most affected babies. Very severe disease linked with blood group mismatch may need exchange transfusion.

vis.caption: Bhutani nomogram for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, guiding phototherapy and exchange transfusion decisions

steps.tx: Babies born to diabetic mothers, small babies and preterm babies face a high risk of **hypoglycaemia** in the first days. A level **under 45** needs treatment, and feeding comes first when the baby can feed safely. Recurrent low values need intravenous dextrose, and persistent **hyperinsulinism** may respond to diazoxide. Repeated heel prick checks guide treatment and protect the developing brain from injury.
steps.say: Some newborn babies cannot keep a safe blood sugar level after birth. Babies of diabetic mothers and small or early babies need regular sugar checks. Feeding treats a low value when the baby can suck and swallow safely. Repeated low values need sugar given directly into a vein. Very persistent cases suggest excess insulin secretion and need specialist investigation.

steps.tx: This photograph shows a **heel prick** sample with a blood drop applied to a **glucometer** strip in a newborn. Bedside testing matters because **hypoglycaemia** can injure the brain while early signs stay nonspecific. At risk babies need scheduled checks rather than a single reading. For the exam, connect the heel prick method with feeding first and intravenous dextrose when low values recur.
steps.say: The photograph shows blood taken from the heel of a wrapped newborn baby. A small drop touches the strip that sits inside the bedside measuring device. This simple test identifies low blood sugar before serious brain injury develops. Babies at high risk need repeated checks during the first days of life. The image reminds you that early feeding and prompt treatment protect the brain.

vis.caption: Neonatal heel prick blood sampling for glucometer testing. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **TORCH** group links rubella with cataract and heart disease, and cytomegalovirus with microcephaly and periventricular calcification. Toxoplasma causes hydrocephalus with chorioretinitis, while syphilis causes snuffles and abnormal teeth. Maternal antibody crosses the placenta, so **neonatal IgM** helps to prove infection in the baby. Early recognition guides treatment, hearing checks and long term follow up.
steps.say: Some infections pass from the mother to the baby before or during birth. Each organism tends to injure a different organ system in the growing baby. Eye disease, heart disease and abnormal head growth form useful exam patterns. Antibody that crosses the placenta comes from the mother and confuses simple testing. Finding antibody made by the baby gives stronger evidence of true infection.
